Market (S&P 500 daily closes): busy days and calm days¶

Notebook for Section 3. Every number the chapter quotes is printed here, and every data figure is drawn here from the real prices. It runs top to bottom on its own (only numpy and matplotlib): open it and Run All, or read it without running anything. We take one column of prices, build a task from it, and walk the five stations of the recipe, meeting a hidden bet at three of them.

Aims of this notebook

  • Build the same small neural network (an MLP) from scratch in numpy and turn one column of prices into a busy-vs-calm task.
  • Run the standard recipe and get a proud-looking score, then cross-examine it station by station.
  • Catch three hidden bets in turn: the split (leak), the scaler (drift), and the yardstick (the moving bar).
  • Along the way: derive the network's gradients by hand and check them against finite differences.

Reproducibility: every experiment seeds its own generator with np.random.default_rng(...), so a fresh Run All reproduces every number below exactly. Run it from the repository root (the data path also resolves from notebooks/).

a. Reading the problem¶

All we are handed is one column: the daily close of the S&P 500. A raw price means nothing across decades, so we turn each day into how much it moved, then keep only the size of the move. The task: from the last five sizes, is tomorrow busier than usual? "Usual" is the middle day, so the two classes are 50/50 and a blind guess is a coin at 0.5.

First the tools and the house style shared by every chapter's figures, and the paths to the data and the figure folder (anchored so they resolve whether we run from the repository root or from notebooks/).

In [1]:

A shape check, our habit before touching anything: how many days did we get?

In [4]:
close.shape
Out[4]:
(6664,)

A raw price means nothing across decades, so we turn each day into how much it moved, then keep only the size of the move. Writing $c_t$ for the close on day $t$,

$$r_t = \frac{c_t - c_{t-1}}{c_{t-1}} \quad\text{(the day's move, a fraction)}, \qquad s_t = |r_t| \quad\text{(its size, forgetting up or down)}.$$

The code uses the same names: daily_return is $r_t$, move_size is $s_t$.

In [5]:
# --- turn each raw price into how much it MOVED, then the SIZE of that move ---
daily_return = np.diff(close) / close[:-1]     # the daily move, as a fraction (a percent)
move_size = np.abs(daily_return)               # the SIZE of the move, forgetting up or down
print("trace, one day at a time:")
for t in range(1, 6):
    print(f"  day {t}: close {close[t]:.2f}  ->  moved {daily_return[t-1]*100:+.2f}%  ->  size {move_size[t-1]*100:.2f}%")

trace, one day at a time:
  day 1: close 1399.42  ->  moved -3.83%  ->  size 3.83%
  day 2: close 1402.11  ->  moved +0.19%  ->  size 0.19%
  day 3: close 1403.45  ->  moved +0.10%  ->  size 0.10%
  day 4: close 1441.47  ->  moved +2.71%  ->  size 2.71%
  day 5: close 1457.60  ->  moved +1.12%  ->  size 1.12%

Is there any signal in these sizes at all? The one honest hope is volatility clustering: a busy day tends to be followed by another busy day. We can read it off directly as the lag-1 autocorrelation of the move sizes, $\mathrm{corr}(s_t,\, s_{t-1})$: a positive value means today's size carries information about tomorrow's.

In [6]:
# --- the volatility-clustering signal: lag-1 autocorrelation of the move sizes ---
acf1_move_size = float(np.corrcoef(move_size[:-1], move_size[1:])[0, 1])
print(f"lag-1 autocorrelation of |r| (the move sizes): {acf1_move_size:+.3f}")
print("  positive -> a busy day tends to be followed by another: a real pattern to try to learn")

lag-1 autocorrelation of |r| (the move sizes): +0.287
  positive -> a busy day tends to be followed by another: a real pattern to try to learn

The task: from the last five sizes, is tomorrow busier than usual? We stack each day's previous five sizes into a feature row, and label it by whether tomorrow's size clears the median. "Usual" is the middle day, so

$$\text{busy}_t = \big[\, s_{t+1} > \mathrm{median}(s)\,\big],$$

which makes the two classes 50/50 by construction: a blind guess is a coin at 0.5.

In [7]:
# --- the task: from the last five sizes, is TOMORROW a busy day (bigger than usual)? ---
N_LAGS = 5
X = np.column_stack([move_size[i:len(move_size) - N_LAGS + i] for i in range(N_LAGS)])
future = move_size[N_LAGS:]; X = X[:len(future)]
usual = float(np.median(move_size))         # "usual" = the middle day; half above, half below
y = (future > usual).astype(int)
print(f"'usual' move size (the middle day): {usual*100:.2f}%   -> the busy / calm line")
print("one row X[0] = the five sizes:", [f"{v*100:.2f}%" for v in X[0]])
print("        its answer = is tomorrow busier than usual? ->", "busy" if y[0] else "calm")
print(f"rows: {len(y)}   busy share: {y.mean():.3f}  (so a blind guess scores 0.5, a coin)")

b. By the book¶

We keep the same little network from Section 1, nothing tuned or added, and run the standard recipe: shuffle the days into train / validation / test, standardize on the training years, train by plain gradient descent, and score accuracy on the sealed test. Loan taught us to cross-examine accuracy first, but here the classes are 50/50, so there is no majority to hide behind and accuracy is an honest judge. So we run it.

The forward pass. For a batch of standardized feature rows $X$ the network computes

$$z_1 = X W_1 + b_1, \qquad h = \max(0,\, z_1)\ \text{(ReLU)}, \qquad z_2 = h W_2 + b_2, \qquad \hat y = \mathrm{softmax}(z_2),$$

and training minimises the cross-entropy loss $J = -\frac{1}{m}\sum_i \log \hat y_{i,\,y_i}$, the average surprise at the true label. In the code logits is $z_2$ and probs is $\hat y$.

The network, defined in one-idea pieces. init_params draws small random weights.

In [10]:
def init_params(dim, width, K, rng):
    return [rng.standard_normal((dim, width))*0.1, np.zeros(width),
            rng.standard_normal((width, K))*0.1, np.zeros(K)]

forward runs $X \to z_1 \to h \to z_2$ and returns all three (we need $z_1$ again for the backward pass).

In [11]:
def forward(Xb, params):
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = params
    pre1 = Xb @ W1 + b1
    hidden = np.maximum(pre1, 0.0)
    logits = hidden @ W2 + b2
    return pre1, hidden, logits

softmax turns logits into probabilities over {calm, busy}.

In [12]:
def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(1, keepdims=True); e = np.exp(z); return e / e.sum(1, keepdims=True)

Two small helpers: accuracy is the fraction predicted correctly, and standardize fits the mean and spread on the training part only and applies them to both parts, so the test set never leaks into the scaling.

In [13]:
def accuracy(params, Xb, yb):
    return float((forward(Xb, params)[2].argmax(1) == yb).mean())
def standardize(Xtr, Xte):
    m, sd = Xtr.mean(0), Xtr.std(0) + 1e-9
    return (Xtr - m) / sd, (Xte - m) / sd

The hyperparameters, surfaced once as named constants so every experiment below reads the same knobs.

In [14]:
WIDTH, LR, EPOCHS, K = 16, 0.3, 300, 2      # MLP width, learning rate, passes, classes
N_SEEDS = 5                                  # random restarts averaged over
seeds = range(N_SEEDS)

Building the task, once. One make_dataset turns the price column into a lag matrix and its label. feature chooses what goes into the rows, the size in percent (the busy/calm task), the size in raw points (same task, a drift-prone unit we abuse later), or the signed direction; the label is the busy/calm cut except for direction, which asks up-or-down. It folds together what used to be three near-identical builders.

In [15]:
def make_dataset(feature="percent"):
    daily_return = np.diff(close) / close[:-1]
    move_size = np.abs(daily_return)                       # size in percent
    if feature == "points":
        source = np.abs(np.diff(close))                    # size in points: drifts with the index level
    elif feature == "direction":
        source = daily_return                              # signed move
    else:
        source = move_size                                 # size in percent
    feats = np.column_stack([source[i:len(source) - N_LAGS + i] for i in range(N_LAGS)])
    if feature == "direction":
        fut = daily_return[N_LAGS:]; feats = feats[:len(fut)]
        labels = (fut > 0).astype(int)                     # up / down, a coin
    else:
        fut = move_size[N_LAGS:]; feats = feats[:len(fut)]
        labels = (fut > np.median(move_size)).astype(int)  # busy / calm, always from the percent size
    return feats, labels

The split, one function with a how switch. A shuffle deals the rows at random; chronological cuts them past -> future (learn on the early years, test on the latest), the honest way the world deals time. 20% test, a 20% validation slice reserved, 60% train.

In [16]:
def split_idx(n, how, seed):
    ntest = n // 5; nval = n // 5                          # 20% test, 20% val (reserved), 60% train
    if how == "chronological":
        test = np.arange(n - ntest, n)
        train = np.arange(0, n - ntest - nval)             # first 60% -> last 20%
    else:
        idx = np.random.default_rng(1000 + seed).permutation(n)
        test = idx[:ntest]; train = idx[ntest + nval:]     # random 60% -> random 20%
    return train, test

The backward pass, by hand. We derive the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, one chain-rule step per line, and wrap it in a single gradients function so the training loop and the learning-curve loop share the same backward pass instead of copying it twice. Two facts do the work: for softmax with cross-entropy the gradient at the logits is simply $\partial J/\partial z_2 = (\hat y - Y)/m$ (with $Y$ the one-hot label), and ReLU passes the gradient straight through wherever its input was positive and blocks it elsewhere. Every gradient variable is named dJ_d_<thing> so the code reads like the chain rule.

In [17]:
def gradients(params, Xb, Y):
    # FORWARD
    pre1, hidden, logits = forward(Xb, params)
    probs = softmax(logits)
    # BACKWARD  (one chain-rule step per line)
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = params
    dJ_d_logits = (probs - Y) / len(Y)          # softmax + cross-entropy gradient at the logits
    dJ_d_W2     = hidden.T @ dJ_d_logits
    dJ_d_b2     = dJ_d_logits.sum(0)            # bias adds to the logits, so its gradient is dJ_d_logits summed
    dJ_d_hidden = dJ_d_logits @ W2.T
    dJ_d_pre1   = dJ_d_hidden * (pre1 > 0)      # ReLU: gradient passes only where the input was positive
    dJ_d_W1     = Xb.T @ dJ_d_pre1
    dJ_d_b1     = dJ_d_pre1.sum(0)
    return dJ_d_W1, dJ_d_b1, dJ_d_W2, dJ_d_b2

One training step, unrolled, on the busy/calm data, to show the mechanism before we hide it in a loop.

In [18]:
# --- ONE training step, unrolled, on a shuffle split of the volatility task ---
Xv, yv = make_dataset("percent")
tr_demo, te_demo = split_idx(len(yv), "shuffle", 0)
Xtr_demo, Xte_demo = standardize(Xv[tr_demo], Xv[te_demo])
ytr_demo = yv[tr_demo]
params = init_params(Xtr_demo.shape[1], WIDTH, K, np.random.default_rng(1))
m = len(ytr_demo); Y = np.zeros((m, K)); Y[np.arange(m), ytr_demo] = 1.0   # one-hot targets

pre1, hidden, logits = forward(Xtr_demo, params)
probs = softmax(logits)
loss_before = -np.log(probs[np.arange(m), ytr_demo] + 1e-12).mean()
dJ_d_W1, dJ_d_b1, dJ_d_W2, dJ_d_b2 = gradients(params, Xtr_demo, Y)
print("loss before one step:", round(float(loss_before), 4),
      " | gradient shapes:", dJ_d_W1.shape, dJ_d_W2.shape)

loss before one step: 0.6972  | gradient shapes: (5, 16) (16, 2)

Do the hand-derived gradients agree with the definition? The surest check is finite differences: nudge one weight by $\pm\delta$, recompute the loss both ways, and compare $(J_+-J_-)/2\delta$ against the analytic gradient. If our chain rule is right they match to several decimals. (This is exactly how real backprop bugs get caught.)

In [19]:
# --- finite-difference gradient check: the textbook relative-error test ---
def cross_entropy(params, Xb, yb):
    p = softmax(forward(Xb, params)[2]); m = len(yb)
    return float(-np.log(p[np.arange(m), yb] + 1e-12).mean())

analytic = {"W1": dJ_d_W1, "b1": dJ_d_b1, "W2": dJ_d_W2, "b2": dJ_d_b2}
delta = 1e-6; rng_check = np.random.default_rng(0)
ana_all, num_all = [], []
print("gradient check  (analytic vs finite difference, relative error per parameter)")
for name, P in zip(["W1", "b1", "W2", "b2"], params):
    flat = P.ravel(); g = analytic[name].ravel()
    sample = rng_check.choice(flat.size, size=min(25, flat.size), replace=False)
    a_s, n_s = [], []
    for k in sample:
        orig = flat[k]
        flat[k] = orig + delta; J_plus  = cross_entropy(params, Xtr_demo, ytr_demo)
        flat[k] = orig - delta; J_minus = cross_entropy(params, Xtr_demo, ytr_demo)
        flat[k] = orig
        a_s.append(g[k]); n_s.append((J_plus - J_minus) / (2*delta))
    a_s, n_s = np.array(a_s), np.array(n_s)
    rel = np.linalg.norm(a_s - n_s) / (np.linalg.norm(a_s) + np.linalg.norm(n_s) + 1e-12)
    ana_all += a_s.tolist(); num_all += n_s.tolist()
    print(f"  {name:3s}: {len(sample):2d} sampled entries, relative error {rel:.2e}")
ana_all, num_all = np.array(ana_all), np.array(num_all)
overall = np.linalg.norm(ana_all - num_all) / (np.linalg.norm(ana_all) + np.linalg.norm(num_all) + 1e-12)
assert overall < 1e-5, "gradient check failed: analytic and numeric gradients disagree"
print(f"  overall relative error {overall:.2e}  ->  the hand-derived backward pass is correct (< 1e-5 passes).")

gradient check  (analytic vs finite difference, relative error per parameter)
  W1 : 25 sampled entries, relative error 5.09e-09
  b1 : 16 sampled entries, relative error 6.28e-09
  W2 : 25 sampled entries, relative error 2.59e-09
  b2 :  2 sampled entries, relative error 2.65e-09
  overall relative error 3.70e-09  ->  the hand-derived backward pass is correct (< 1e-5 passes).

Now wrap that same forward-and-backward into a training loop. train calls the shared gradients each epoch and takes one plain gradient-descent step.

In [20]:
def train(Xtr, ytr, width, lr, epochs, K, rng):
    params = init_params(Xtr.shape[1], width, K, rng)
    n = len(ytr); Y = np.zeros((n, K)); Y[np.arange(n), ytr] = 1.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        dJ_d_W1, dJ_d_b1, dJ_d_W2, dJ_d_b2 = gradients(params, Xtr, Y)
        W1, b1, W2, b2 = params
        params = [W1 - lr*dJ_d_W1, b1 - lr*dJ_d_b1, W2 - lr*dJ_d_W2, b2 - lr*dJ_d_b2]
    return params

Two scoring helpers. score_split splits, standardizes, trains, and returns the sealed-test accuracy for one seed. walk_forward grows the training window fold by fold, always testing on the next block, the rolling version of the honest split.

In [21]:
def score_split(Xf, yf, how, seed, lr=LR):
    tr, te = split_idx(len(yf), how, seed)
    Xtr, Xte = standardize(Xf[tr], Xf[te])
    params = train(Xtr, yf[tr], WIDTH, lr, EPOCHS, K, np.random.default_rng(seed))
    return accuracy(params, Xte, yf[te])
In [22]:
def walk_forward(Xf, yf, folds=5, lr=LR):
    n = len(yf); bs = n // (folds + 1); out = []
    for k in range(1, folds + 1):
        tr = np.arange(0, k*bs); te = np.arange(k*bs, (k+1)*bs)
        Xtr, Xte = standardize(Xf[tr], Xf[te])
        params = train(Xtr, yf[tr], WIDTH, lr, EPOCHS, K, np.random.default_rng(k))
        out.append(accuracy(params, Xte, yf[te]))
    return float(np.mean(out)), out

Predict the number before running. The classes are 50/50, so a blind coin scores 0.5. Run the by-the-book recipe, a shuffle split, over the five seeds and read the score.

In [23]:
vol_shuffle_accs = [score_split(Xv, yv, "shuffle", s) for s in seeds]
V_SH = float(np.mean(vol_shuffle_accs))
print(f"the score comes back: {V_SH:.3f}   (every shuffle: {[round(x, 3) for x in vol_shuffle_accs]})")

the score comes back: 0.612   (every shuffle: [0.607, 0.624, 0.621, 0.618, 0.59])

Against a blind coin at 0.5, that is about eleven points of something. Whether it is skill or an artefact is the whole question of this chapter.

Can we trust that number? If it is lying, the lie sits at one of the five stations. Three we can check right now.

  1. The build. Did the network actually learn, or is this a lucky roll?
  2. The measure. Is it deciding both ways, or just parroting one class?
  3. The split. Was the exam fair, or did we draw a lucky test set?

Two stations at once: did the model actually learn (climb from a coin), and is it deciding both ways rather than parroting one class? We average over the five seeds so no single lucky start can flatter the picture. The loop reuses the same gradients as train.

In [24]:
def learning_curves(Xf, yf, seeds=range(N_SEEDS), how="shuffle", lr=LR, epochs=EPOCHS, width=WIDTH, every=5):
    marks = [0] + [e for e in range(1, epochs+1) if e <= 20 or e % every == 0]
    mset = set(marks); runs, bshare, bhit, chit = [], [], [], []
    for s in seeds:
        tr, te = split_idx(len(yf), how, s)
        Xtr, Xte = standardize(Xf[tr], Xf[te]); ytr, yte = yf[tr], yf[te]
        p = init_params(Xtr.shape[1], width, K, np.random.default_rng(s)); n = len(ytr)
        Y = np.zeros((n, K)); Y[np.arange(n), ytr] = 1.0
        got = {0: accuracy(p, Xtr, ytr)}                    # epoch 0: untrained weights
        for e in range(1, epochs+1):
            dJ_d_W1, dJ_d_b1, dJ_d_W2, dJ_d_b2 = gradients(p, Xtr, Y)
            W1, b1, W2, b2 = p
            p = [W1 - lr*dJ_d_W1, b1 - lr*dJ_d_b1, W2 - lr*dJ_d_W2, b2 - lr*dJ_d_b2]
            if e in mset: got[e] = accuracy(p, Xtr, ytr)
        runs.append([got[mk] for mk in marks])
        pr = forward(Xte, p)[2].argmax(1)
        bshare.append(float(pr.mean()))
        bhit.append(float((pr[yte == 1] == 1).mean())); chit.append(float((pr[yte == 0] == 0).mean()))
    return marks, np.mean(runs, 0), np.mean(bshare), np.mean(bhit), np.mean(chit)

Run it and read the two answers: the training curve from untrained to settled, and what the model does on the sealed test (how often it says busy, and how many of each class it gets right).

In [25]:
marks, curve, bshare, bhit, chit = learning_curves(Xv, yv)
print(f"training accuracy (mean of 5 seeds): {curve[0]:.3f} untrained  ->  {curve[-1]:.3f} settled")
print("\nis it doing something real, or just parroting one class?")
print(f"  on the sealed test it answers BUSY {bshare:.3f} of the time, CALM {1-bshare:.3f}")
print(f"  it gets {bhit:.3f} of the busy days right, and {chit:.3f} of the calm days right")

All three come back clean: it climbs from a coin and settles, it calls both classes, and the score barely moves across shuffles. So we trust it. But look at what we did to clear the split: we shuffled and scored, five times over. That is one check run five times, not five checks. So we check it a genuinely different way.

c. So was it the shuffle?¶

Nobody in real life shuffles time. We cut the days the way the world deals them: learn from the early years, test on the latest years, sealed.

We cut the days the honest way, past -> future, and compare it to the shuffle on the same task. As a control we run a task with no pattern to steal, up-or-down direction, where a leak should have nothing to feed on.

Same model, same days, only which day went into which pile changed, and the honest score falls by more than two points. The reason is in the rows: each window slides along one day, so neighbours share four of their five numbers. Shuffle those near-twins and a row's twin can sit in training while the row sits in the test, so the model recognises the answer instead of predicting it. The control confirms it: on up-or-down, a task with no pattern, the gap vanishes.

Hidden assumption: the days are interchangeable. What else have we only ever checked one way?

d. And what about the scaling?¶

We measured the mean and the spread once, on the training years, and used them forever. That is a bet: that a normal day stays normal. We never checked it. To see a bet like that, we watch it lose. We feed the same task the size of each move in raw points instead of percent, a feature whose normal really does drift as the index climbs, and change nothing else.

The scaler, tested by watching it lose. The idea: a frozen scaler is just two numbers (a mean and a spread) measured once on the training years and used forever. Two helpers do the scaling, standardize (the frozen scaler we already have) and a rolling_z that rescales each row by its own trailing window.

In [30]:
def rolling_z(Xf, W=250):                                        # each row scaled by its own trailing window
    Z = np.zeros_like(Xf)
    for j in range(Xf.shape[1]):
        c = Xf[:, j]
        cs = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(c)]); cs2 = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(c*c)])
        for t in range(len(c)):
            lo = max(0, t-W); mm = t-lo
            if mm < 30: continue
            mu = (cs[t]-cs[lo])/mm; var = (cs2[t]-cs2[lo])/mm - mu*mu
            Z[t, j] = (c[t]-mu)/(np.sqrt(max(var, 1e-18))+1e-9)
    return Z

score_scaling runs the honest past -> future split (split_idx(..., "chronological", ...), in place of the old bespoke chron_idx) with either scaler, on the size in percent or in points. The frozen scaler is standardize; the old frozen helper was the very same two lines, so we drop it.

In [31]:
def score_scaling(kind, scaler, seeds=range(N_SEEDS), lr=LR):
    Xf, yf = make_dataset(kind); nn = len(yf)
    tr, te = split_idx(nn, "chronological", 0)
    if scaler == "frozen":
        Xtr, Xte = standardize(Xf[tr], Xf[te])
    else:
        Z = rolling_z(Xf); Xtr, Xte = Z[tr], Z[te]
    a = [accuracy(train(Xtr, yf[tr], WIDTH, lr, EPOCHS, K, np.random.default_rng(s)), Xte, yf[te]) for s in seeds]
    return float(np.mean(a))

Change only the feature's unit and the scaler, nothing else, and read the three scores.

In [32]:

PTS_ROLL = score_scaling("points", "rolling")

Same days, same task, same honest split. Only the unit and the scaler change:
  size in percent + frozen scaler : 0.587
  size in points  + frozen scaler : 0.509   <- a coin
  size in points  + rolling scaler: 0.528

Why does points collapse? Because the frozen scaler's idea of a normal day is fixed at the training years, while a normal day in points drifts as the index climbs. The loop below prints, for each unit, the frozen normal, what a normal day actually drifted to, and how far the test days now land from that frozen normal.

In [33]:
print("\nthe frozen scaler is two numbers taken once, on the training years, then used forever:")
for kind in ("percent", "points"):
    Xf, yf = make_dataset(kind); tr, te = split_idx(len(yf), "chronological", 0)
    col = Xf[:, -1].astype(float) * (100 if kind == "percent" else 1)   # most recent day's size in each row
    m_tr, s_tr = col[tr].mean(), col[tr].std()                          # the mean and std we froze
    m_te = col[te].mean()                                              # what a normal day actually became
    _, Xte = standardize(Xf[tr], Xf[te]); unit = "%" if kind == "percent" else " pts"
    print(f"  {kind}: froze normal at mean {m_tr:.2f}{unit} (spread {s_tr:.2f}); by the test years it had drifted to {m_te:.2f}{unit}  (x{m_te/m_tr:.1f})")
    print(f"          so the test days land at |z| mean {np.abs(Xte).mean():.2f}, max {np.abs(Xte).max():.2f} from the frozen normal")

In points the model drops to a coin. Over these years the index roughly five-folds (the price climbs about x5), and a normal day's size in points drifts along with it, from about 10.6 points to 37 points, a ~x3.5 move in what counts as normal. So every test day now arrives looking like a wild outlier measured against the frozen normal. Percent survives only because it drifts a little (x0.9), not because it is safe, and even a smarter rolling scaler cannot bring points back to the honest 0.587.

Hidden assumption: the world stands still. So we rebuild the whole plan with our eyes open, and this time every station is checked. One last check first: was the slice of time we tested on special?

e. The process we can finally trust¶

We run the very same honest test, train on the past and test on what comes next, but at five points spaced along the history instead of only at the end. Same recipe, five different moments in time.

Run the honest past -> future test at five points spaced along the history, and against each era's own lazy bar (whichever class has been common lately), not a flat 0.5.

In [36]:
# ---- BOOM 2: the number we KEPT. Does it hold still, and what is the right bar in each era? ----
bs = len(yv)//6
eras = []
for k in range(1, 6):
    tr = np.arange(0, k*bs); te = np.arange(k*bs, (k+1)*bs)
    Xtr, Xte = standardize(Xv[tr], Xv[te])
    a = float(np.mean([accuracy(train(Xtr, yv[tr], 16, 0.3, 300, 2, np.random.default_rng(s)), Xte, yv[te])
                       for s in range(5)]))
    busy = float(yv[te].mean()); base = max(busy, 1-busy)
    eras.append((k, a, busy, base, a-base))
    print(f"era {k}: model {a:.3f}   busy share {busy:.3f}   the bar that era sets {base:.3f}   margin {a-base:+.3f}")

accs = [e[1] for e in eras]; marg = [e[4] for e in eras]
se = float(np.sqrt(0.6*0.4/bs))
print(f"\nacross eras the score runs {min(accs):.3f} to {max(accs):.3f}, a spread of {max(accs)-min(accs):.3f}")
print(f"sampling noise on a {bs}-day block is about {se:.3f}, so the swing is {(max(accs)-min(accs))/se:.1f}x noise")
print(f"margin over the bar each era actually sets: mean {np.mean(marg):+.3f}, from {min(marg):+.3f} to {max(marg):+.3f}")
print(f"the headline was 0.612 against a flat coin, which read as +{0.612-0.5:.3f}")

            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#c85a52", lw=1.2))
ax.text((min(accs)+max(accs))/2, 0.46, f"the same model, era by era: {min(accs):.3f} to {max(accs):.3f}",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10, color="#b04a42")
ax.set_xlim(0.47, 0.70); ax.set_ylim(0.15, 3.15)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("accuracy on the sealed test days")
ax.set_title("We came to confirm one number, and found five that disagree", loc="left", fontsize=12, color="#2b333f")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False); ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False); ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=GRID, linewidth=1); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(f"{FIG}/market_spread.svg", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

The five do not agree: the model runs from barely a coin to genuinely good, a swing about nine times sampling noise, so there was never one number. And the bar itself drifts. The fair bar is not a flat 0.5 but a lazy guesser who always plays whichever class has been common lately, and how well that scores changes era to era (the busy share drifts from 0.37 to 0.54). Marked against each era's own bar, the model's lead is about +0.05 on average, not the +0.112 the headline implied, and in one era it is beaten outright.

Hidden assumption: the yardstick stands still. And it hid in station one, Frame, the one step we never put on any suspect list, because setting the exam never felt like a step we could get wrong.

f. So what did all that teach us?¶

Three times a healthy-looking number hid a bet we had run on faith:

  • Split bet the days were interchangeable (leak): the shuffle's 0.612 was memory; honest, it is 0.587.
  • Scale bet a normal day stays normal (drift): in points it fell to 0.509.
  • Frame bet the question and the bar were simply given: judged era by era, the real edge is about +0.05, not the +0.112 headline.

The recipe was never a list of steps to run. It is a list of bets to read. The full landing is in Section 3f of the report.
